nodes.displayName: 加减法应用题 · 10以内的情境

nodes.sourceName: Finding a missing number in addition

nodes.description: Fluently add and subtract within 10

nodes.description: Create and compare different representations of the same data set (table, scaled pictograph, bar graph), including with software, interpret the data in context, and choose the representation that best suits a purpose

Enter the same data into a spreadsheet with one column for the category and one for the count

Find the difference in rainfall between two months from a line graph

Complete a two-way table from given data about favourite sports by gender
Calculate how long a train journey takes using a timetable

Use 'outlier' correctly to identify a value that doesn't fit the pattern, and explain its effect on the mean
Use 'correlation' correctly when describing the relationship shown in a scatter graph

Find a missing data value given the mean and all other values

Construct a line graph from a table of continuous data, choosing an appropriate scale and labelling axes correctly
Use a line graph to solve a two-step problem, such as finding the time period with the greatest rate of change

Construct a pie chart from given data by calculating sector angles
Use a pie chart to determine the actual quantity represented by each sector given the total
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a pie chart — for example, one showing how a family spends its weekly budget — and use it to answer questions and solve problems?

Choose and justify a display (column graph, dot plot or table) for the collected data
Write a short report that answers the question and states one limitation of the data

Classify 'favourite colour' as nominal and 'rating from 1 to 5' as ordinal and explain the difference
Use spreadsheet formulas to total each category, then report the mode and describe the shape of the column graph
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} collects survey answers in a spreadsheet, can they spot entries that don't make sense, total each category, and describe what the most common answer was?

nodes.description: Calculate the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of a small numerical data set — find the mean, find each value's distance from the mean (a non-negative number: a value equal to the mean has distance 0), then find the mean of those distances; interpret the MAD as the average distance of the values from the mean, stated in the original units of the data (e.g. minutes, cm, points); and use MADs to compare the spread or consistency of two data sets, recognising that a larger MAD means values typically sit further from the mean and that the MAD is 0 only when every value equals the mean
evidence: Calculate the MAD of 4, 6, 8, 9, 13 (mean 8; distances 4, 2, 0, 1, 5; MAD 2.4), counting the value equal to the mean as a distance of 0
Explain that a MAD of 3 cm for a set of plant heights means the heights are, on average, 3 cm away from the mean height
Decide which of two bowlers, both with a mean score of 120, is more consistent when their MADs are 8 and 21 points, and justify the choice
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wrote down how many minutes late the school bus was each day for a week, could they work out how far each day was from the average lateness, average those distances, and explain what that number says about how reliable the bus is?

nodes.description: Describe, interpret, and compare observed distributions of a single variable using measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and spread (range), including choosing a suitable average and the effect of outliers; comparisons describe the observed data sets themselves and do not yet scale the difference in centres by a measure of variability or generalise from samples to wider populations
evidence: Find the mean, median and mode of 3, 5, 5, 6, 11 (6, 5 and 5) and say which average best represents a typical value
Find the range of 12, 14, 15, 15, 48 and explain why the outlier 48 pulls the mean (20.8) well above the median (15)
Compare two classes' spelling scores using their medians and ranges and write one conclusion about which class did better and one about which was more consistent
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had the test scores of a whole class, could they find the mean, median, and range, and explain what each tells you about how the class performed?

nodes.description: Construct and interpret a box plot on a numerical scale from a five-number summary (minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, maximum), using the stated convention that the whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values; interpret the median, quartiles, IQR and range, recognising that each whisker and each half of the box represents roughly a quarter of the data however long or short it is drawn; explain what a box plot does not show (individual values, clusters, gaps, the number of values, or the mean); and compare two distributions using their box plots
evidence: Draw a box plot for the five-number summary 3, 6, 9, 14, 21 on a labelled scale, stating that the whiskers run from the minimum to the maximum, and read the median, quartiles, IQR (8) and range (18) back from a given box plot

Explain that the longer upper whisker (from 14 to 21) shows the top quarter of values is more spread out — not that it contains more values — and reject claims a box plot cannot support, such as 'the mean is 9', 'most values are close to 9' or the exact number of data values

Explain with an example how two data sets can have the same box plot but different shapes (e.g. one with values spread evenly, the other with two clusters separated by a gap), and compare two classes' box plots using their medians and IQRs in context
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees box plots comparing how long two classes spent on homework, could they say which class had the higher middle time and which was more spread out — and explain why a longer whisker doesn't mean more children are in that part?

nodes.description: Interpret and compare data sets for nominal and ordinal categorical and discrete and continuous numerical variables using comparative displays (side-by-side column graphs with ordinal categories in a common order, back-to-back dot plots) made with digital tools, processing the data (percentages, ranges) and comparing distributions by mode, range and shape
evidence: Make a side-by-side column graph in a spreadsheet comparing the favourite sports (nominal) of Year 3 and Year 6 students and state the mode for each group

Compare two classes' ratings of 'How much do you enjoy reading?' (never, sometimes, often, always) as percentages on side-by-side graphs with the categories in the same order, and say which class's ratings sit higher on the scale
Compare two classes' jump distances by mode, range and shape using back-to-back dot plots made with a digital tool
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has survey results from two classes of different sizes, can they use a spreadsheet to make a side-by-side graph, turn the counts into percentages, and compare the two fairly?

nodes.description: Identify statistically informed arguments in traditional and digital media and critique their methods, data representations (e.g. truncated axes, distorted pictographs, selective data) and conclusions
evidence: Explain how a bar graph whose vertical axis starts at 90 exaggerates a small difference
Identify the sample size and who was surveyed in a news claim such as '9 out of 10 kids prefer Brand X' and judge whether the conclusion is justified
Rewrite a misleading online headline so that it matches what the data actually show
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an ad saying '9 out of 10 kids prefer this cereal' or a graph with a stretched-out axis, can they ask who was asked and whether the graph makes the difference look bigger than it is?

nodes.description: Describe the distribution of a numerical data set by its centre, spread and overall shape — recognising clusters, gaps, peaks, symmetry or skew (a longer tail on one side) and unusual values — and interpret each feature in the context in which the data were collected, recognising that distributions with similar centres can differ greatly in spread and shape
evidence: Describe a dot plot of 25 pupils' reaction times by its centre (a typical value), its spread (where most values lie and how far they extend) and its shape — naming any cluster, gap, symmetry or skew and unusual value — and link each feature to the context (e.g. a gap between two groups of times might reflect pupils who had practised and pupils who had not)

Compare two distributions with the same mean — e.g. two classes both averaging 60% on a test, one with scores clustered between 52% and 68%, the other spread from 20% to 95% in two separate clusters — and explain what the shared mean hides and why the difference matters in context

Use the context to judge whether an unusual value is more likely a recording error or a genuine extreme (e.g. a reaction time of 4.2 s among times near 0.3 s), and identify claims the display alone cannot support, such as the reason for a skew or that the same pattern would hold for a different group
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a dot plot of how long children in their class took to run 100 m, could they describe where most times bunch up, how spread out they are and whether there are any odd ones out — and suggest a sensible reason for what they see?

nodes.description: Construct and interpret dot plots for numerical data sets of any kind (counts, scores, times or measurements), extending earlier measurement line plots: draw a number-line scale with equal intervals that runs from at least the minimum to the maximum value, including values nobody recorded so that gaps stay visible; place one dot per observation, stacking repeated values in evenly spaced columns; label the scale with the attribute and its units; and read the plot to find how often a value occurs, the minimum, maximum and most common values, and the total number of observations, recognising that the height of a stack is a count of observations, not a data value
evidence: Draw a dot plot of 20 pupils' numbers of books read last month (values 0 to 12) on a scale marked 0, 1, 2, …, 12, leaving the empty value 7 visible as a gap and stacking the four 3s evenly
Read from a dot plot that the value 5 occurs 6 times, the minimum is 0, the maximum is 12 and the most common value is 5
Explain that a stack of 6 dots above 5 means six pupils each read 5 books, not that someone read 6 books, and count all the dots to give the number of pupils
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} asked 20 classmates how many books they read last month, could they draw a dot plot with one dot per person stacked above the right number on a number line — and then say how many classmates read exactly 5 books?

nodes.description: Construct and interpret histograms for continuous or numerical data grouped into equal-width class intervals on a continuous number-line scale, with no gaps between bars; state the interval-boundary convention used (e.g. 140 ≤ h < 150, so a value of exactly 150 belongs to the next interval); read frequencies from bar heights; describe the distribution shown; and explain how a histogram differs from a bar chart of categories. Unequal-width intervals and frequency density are not included.
evidence: Group 30 pupils' heights into equal-width 10 cm intervals (130 ≤ h < 140, 140 ≤ h < 150, …), stating that a height of exactly 150 cm is counted in the 150 ≤ h < 160 interval, and draw the histogram with a continuous horizontal scale, touching bars and labelled axes

Read frequencies accurately from a histogram (e.g. how many pupils are at least 150 cm but less than 160 cm, and how many are shorter than 150 cm in total) and describe the distribution's centre, spread and shape in context

Explain why a histogram's bars touch and sit on a numerical scale while a bar chart of categories (e.g. favourite sport) has gaps and an order that could be rearranged — and identify claims the histogram cannot support, such as the exact height of the tallest pupil or how many pupils are exactly 145 cm tall
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sorted the heights of everyone in their class into groups like '130 cm up to 140 cm' and '140 cm up to 150 cm', could they draw a histogram with the bars touching — and explain why it isn't the same kind of chart as a bar chart of favourite colours?

nodes.description: Construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts, pictograms, and vertical line charts for both categorical and grouped numerical data, choosing appropriate representations for the data type

Draw a pie chart by calculating the angle for each category
Interpret a bar chart comparing two data sets and draw a conclusion about the difference

nodes.description: Distinguish a population from a sample drawn from it; explain why a convenient or biased sample (choosing whoever is easiest to reach, volunteers, or a group linked to the answer) can misrepresent the population; explain that random selection gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen, which tends to produce representative samples — while recognising that any single random sample can still, by chance, be unrepresentative
evidence: In a described survey (e.g. a school asks 40 of its 800 pupils about the lunch menu), identify the population and the sample, and explain why a sample is used instead of asking everyone

Identify the selection bias in a sampling method (e.g. asking people leaving a gym how often they exercise, or surveying only the lunch queue on pizza day), explain the direction in which it would likely distort the result, and propose a better method using random selection from the whole population (e.g. drawing names from the full school register)

Explain the difference between random selection and simply choosing whoever is easiest to reach, and explain — with an example such as a random sample of 10 pupils that happens to contain mostly Year 7s — why random sampling makes a representative sample likely but does not guarantee it

nodes.description: Find the median, lower quartile and upper quartile of a data set using one explicit convention — order the data, find the median, split the data into a lower and an upper half (leaving out the median itself when there is an odd number of values), and take the median of each half as the lower and upper quartile — while recognising that other textbooks, calculators and software may use slightly different conventions; calculate the interquartile range (IQR = upper quartile − lower quartile) and interpret it as the spread of the middle half of the data; and compare what the range and the IQR reveal, including their different sensitivity to extreme values
evidence: Using the stated convention, find the median (9), lower quartile (6, the median of 3, 5, 6, 7, 8) and upper quartile (14, the median of 11, 12, 14, 15, 21) of the 11 values 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 21, giving IQR = 8; and for the 10 values 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, find median 7.5, lower quartile 4 and upper quartile 10, giving IQR = 6

Interpret an IQR in context (e.g. 'the middle half of the puzzle times lie between 6 and 14 minutes, a spread of 8 minutes') and explain that about half of the values lie between the quartiles, with about a quarter below the lower quartile and about a quarter above the upper quartile

Show that changing the largest value from 21 to 40 increases the range from 18 to 37 but leaves the IQR at 8, and use this to decide — and justify — whether the range or the IQR gives the better summary of spread for a data set with an extreme value or a long tail
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} lines up the times their friends took to finish a puzzle, could they find the middle time and the 'quarter-way' times either side of it — and explain why the gap between those quarter-way times is a better guide to how spread out most of the group is than the gap between the very fastest and slowest?

nodes.description: Plan and conduct a full statistical investigation by posing and refining questions or identifying a problem, planning and carrying out data collection, analysing and interpreting the data, and communicating findings in context
evidence: Refine a vague question like 'Do kids like sport?' into 'How many hours of organised sport do Year 6 students play each week?'
Plan and carry out the data collection, recording who was asked, how and when
Analyse the data with a suitable display and summary values and present a conclusion with one suggested improvement to the investigation
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} turn a vague question like 'Do kids like sport?' into a precise one, collect the data, and present a conclusion with a suggestion for doing it better next time?

nodes.description: Distinguish a statistical question — one that anticipates variability in the data collected to answer it, so its answer must account for that variability (even when it is reported as a single summary value such as a mean or median) — from a question answered by a single fixed fact; for a statistical question, identify the population (who or what is being asked about), the attribute being investigated, and the variation expected in the answers
evidence: Sort questions such as 'How tall am I?', 'How tall are the pupils in my class?', 'How many days are in March?' and 'How many hours of sleep do 12-year-olds usually get?' into statistical and non-statistical, explaining each choice by whether the answers are expected to vary

For a given statistical question, name the population and the attribute being measured, describe the variation they expect (e.g. 'sleep times will differ from person to person, perhaps from 7 to 11 hours'), and explain that a good answer must account for that variability in the data — even a single-number summary such as 'a typical 12-year-old sleeps about 9 hours' stands for many differing values, unlike the one fixed answer to 'How many days are in March?'

Explain why a question about a group can still be non-statistical (e.g. 'How many pupils are in my class?' has one fixed answer), and rewrite a non-statistical question as a statistical one (e.g. 'How long is my journey to school?' becomes 'How long are journeys to school for pupils in my year?')
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} whether 'How many pets does our family have?' and 'How many pets do children in your class have?' are the same kind of question, can they explain that the second one has lots of different answers — so you'd need to collect data from many people — while the first has just one answer?

nodes.description: Before summarising a numerical data set, state its context precisely: report the number of observations (n) by counting the values in a list or the dots on a dot plot, or by adding the frequencies in a table or histogram (not by counting rows or bars); describe the attribute investigated (what was measured or counted, and for whom or what), how it was measured (the instrument or method and the precision or rounding used, e.g. measured with a tape to the nearest cm versus self-reported) and its units; and use these details to give every summary value with its units and to judge what the data can show, for example recognising when values bunch at round numbers because of how they were recorded
evidence: Report that a frequency table with frequencies 3, 7, 6 and 4 records 20 observations, not 4 (the number of rows) or 7 (the largest frequency)
Write a context statement such as 'hand spans of 28 pupils, measured with a ruler from thumb tip to little-finger tip, to the nearest 0.5 cm'
Explain that a pile-up of self-reported bedtimes at exactly 9:00 and 9:30 may come from people rounding their answers rather than from real bedtimes
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured classmates' hand spans for a project, could they say exactly how many people were measured, what was measured, how it was measured (e.g. with a ruler to the nearest half centimetre) and in what units — before giving any averages?

nodes.description: Write a complete summary of a numerical data set in relation to its context, bringing together: the number of observations; the attribute, how it was measured and its units; a measure of centre with a matching measure of variability, each with units, chosen between median with IQR and mean with MAD; the overall pattern and any striking deviations, interpreted in context; and a justification of that choice by the shape of the distribution and the context (e.g. median and IQR for skewed data or data with extreme values, mean and MAD for roughly symmetric data without extreme values)
evidence: Write a summary of 25 pupils' reaction times that states n, the attribute, how it was measured and the units, a centre and a matching measure of spread with units, and any unusual value
Choose the median and IQR rather than the mean and MAD for a set of journey times with a long tail of slow journeys, and justify the choice by that tail
Rewrite the summary 'the average is 14' as 'the 30 pupils' median journey time is 14 minutes, with the middle half of times between 9 and 22 minutes'
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} timed how long 25 friends took to solve a puzzle, could they write a short report saying how many were timed, how the times were measured, a typical time and how spread out the times were (with units) — and mention any time that stood out?

nodes.description: Use measures of centre and variability calculated from random samples of two populations to make informal comparative inferences about those populations (e.g. whether words in a Grade 7 science book are generally longer than words in a Grade 4 science book): check that each sample was randomly drawn from the population it is meant to describe and is reasonably representative; weigh the difference between the sample centres against the variability within the samples and against how much centres vary from one random sample to another; and state qualified conclusions ('generally', 'on average', 'probably') rather than claiming every member of one population exceeds every member of the other — recognising that a small difference between two samples may be due to chance alone
evidence: Compare random samples of 20 word lengths from two books (means 6.2 and 4.4 letters, both MADs about 0.9) and conclude that the first book probably uses longer words on average
Explain why surveying volunteers at one school's sports club cannot support a conclusion that all pupils at that school are fitter than pupils at another school
Judge that a 1-point difference between two sample medians is not convincing when repeated random samples from one population give medians that vary by about 3 points
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} randomly picked 20 words from a Year 7 science book and 20 from a Year 4 science book, could they use the averages and spreads to decide whether the older book generally uses longer words — and explain why they'd say 'probably' rather than 'definitely'?

nodes.description: Use data from a random sample to estimate a characteristic of the population, such as a proportion, total count, or mean; present the result as an estimate rather than an exact population measurement; state the assumptions the inference relies on (the sample was randomly drawn from the population being described and is reasonably representative) and explain how the conclusion is limited or invalid when those assumptions fail
evidence: Use a sample proportion to estimate a population count — e.g. 18 of a random sample of 60 pupils walk to school, so estimate about 270 of the school's 900 pupils walk — and state the answer as an approximate estimate rather than an exact count

Use the mean of a random sample (e.g. the mean weekly reading time of 25 randomly chosen pupils) to estimate the population mean, and explain why the true population mean is likely to be close to, but probably not exactly equal to, the sample mean

State the assumptions behind an estimate and explain why it becomes unreliable or invalid when they fail — e.g. using a sample of only Year 7 pupils to estimate for the whole school, or using a volunteer online poll — and identify what can and cannot be concluded from the data
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that 12 out of 40 randomly chosen pupils at their school play an instrument, could they estimate how many of the school's 600 pupils play one — and explain why that number is a sensible estimate rather than an exact count?

nodes.sourceName: How far apart two groups are
nodes.description: Compare two numerical distributions with similar variability shown on a shared scale (e.g. dot plots) in two distinct ways: (1) judge their actual visual overlap directly from the displays — how much of each group's data lies among the other group's values; and (2) separately, find the difference between their centres and express it as a multiple of a clearly named measure of variability of either group, using matching measures (difference in means ÷ MAD, or difference in medians ÷ IQR), interpreting a larger multiple as centres that are further apart relative to the typical spread. Recognise that the same difference in centres means more when the variability is small, and that for similarly shaped, roughly symmetric, single-peaked distributions a larger multiple usually goes with less overlap — but that the ratio alone does not determine overlap: skew, clusters, gaps or outliers can make the visible overlap greater or smaller than the ratio suggests, so overlap is always checked on the display; and this simple ratio is only appropriate when the two variabilities are similar
evidence: Describe two dot plots of team heights drawn on the same scale as overlapping a lot, a little, or hardly at all, pointing to the range of heights the two teams share
Express a 10 cm difference in mean heights as about 2 MADs when each team's MAD is about 5 cm, naming MAD as the measure used
Use two dot plots whose means are 2 MADs apart, one with a long tail towards the other group, to explain why they overlap more than the 2-MAD gap alone would suggest

nodes.description: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or angles of a specified size; recognise right triangles as a category
evidence: Sort a set of quadrilaterals into those with parallel sides and those without
Identify which triangles in a set are right triangles
Classify shapes that have both perpendicular and parallel sides
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a mixed set of triangles and quadrilaterals, can they sort them into groups — like "shapes with at least one right angle" or "shapes with parallel sides" — and explain their reasoning?

nodes.description: Know that angles are measured in degrees, where one degree is 1/360 of a full turn; understand that an angle turning through n one-degree angles has a measure of n degrees
evidence: Explain that a full turn is 360° and a right angle is 90°
Describe what 'one degree' means in terms of a fraction of a circle
State that an angle of 45° has turned through 45 one-degree angles
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a full circle is 360 degrees, can they tell you how many degrees a quarter turn is — and explain roughly what one single degree looks like?

nodes.description: Estimate and compare acute, obtuse, and reflex angles in degrees; classify angles by type and order them by size
evidence: Estimate an angle as approximately 130° and classify it as obtuse
Identify a reflex angle in a diagram and estimate it as about 270°
Order four angles from smallest to largest by estimation before measuring
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} three different angles drawn on paper, can they estimate which is biggest, label each as acute, obtuse, or reflex — and then check with a protractor?

nodes.description: Draw and identify points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines; identify these in two-dimensional figures
evidence: Draw a pair of perpendicular lines and a pair of parallel lines
Identify all pairs of parallel sides in a trapezoid
Mark a right angle, an acute angle, and an obtuse angle in a given figure
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a piece of paper and a ruler, can they draw a line segment, mark a point, and then draw another line through that point that runs perfectly parallel to the first?

nodes.displayName: 测量角 · 量角与画角
nodes.description: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor; draw given angles and sketch angles of specified measure
evidence: Measure an angle with a protractor and read 47°
Draw an angle of 135° using a protractor
Identify which scale on the protractor to use for an obtuse angle
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a protractor and an angle drawn on paper, can they measure it accurately and then draw a new angle of a size you specify?

nodes.description: Recognise angle measure as additive; find unknown angles by adding or subtracting on a diagram using equations with a symbol for the unknown
evidence: Two angles on a straight line are 65° and x°; find x = 115°
An angle is decomposed into 35° and 40°; state the whole angle is 75°
Solve: angles at a point are 120°, 90°, and x°; find x = 150°
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If two angles sit next to each other on a straight line and one is 65°, can {{name}} work out the other angle — knowing that angles on a straight line always add up to 180°?

nodes.sourceTitle: 正多边形与不规则多边形
nodes.displayName: 正多边形与不规则多边形
nodes.description: Distinguish between regular and irregular polygons based on reasoning about equal sides and equal angles
evidence: Classify a set of polygons as regular or irregular
Explain that a regular pentagon has 5 equal sides and 5 equal angles
Identify that a rectangle is irregular (equal angles but not all equal sides) unless it is a square
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a stop sign (regular octagon) and a wonky eight-sided shape, can they explain which is regular and which is irregular — and why?

nodes.description: Recognise rotational symmetry in shapes and designs, state how many times a shape matches itself in a full turn, and create patterns with line and rotational symmetry, including by rotating a motif in dynamic geometry software
evidence: Turn a square tracing and show it fits onto itself 4 times in a full turn
Identify which of a pinwheel, a heart and an equilateral triangle have rotational symmetry
Use dynamic geometry software to rotate a motif by quarter turns about a point to create a design with rotational symmetry of order 4
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} turns a pinwheel or a square tile, can they notice it looks exactly the same after part of a turn — and count how many times that happens in one full turn?

nodes.description: Name, estimate and compare straight angles, reflex angles and revolutions alongside acute, right and obtuse angles, describing each by its relationship to a right angle (without measuring in degrees)
evidence: Identify a straight angle as two right angles and a revolution as four right angles
Sort angles from a set of drawn shapes into acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex
Estimate whether an angle drawn between clock hands is less than or more than a straight angle
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the hands on a clock, can they say whether the angle between them is a straight line, smaller than a right angle, or bigger than a straight line (a reflex angle)?

nodes.displayName: 网格上的图形变换 · 反射与平移后的位置
nodes.description: Identify, describe, and represent the position of a shape following a reflection or translation using appropriate language; know that the shape has not changed
evidence: Reflect a triangle in a vertical mirror line on a coordinate grid and state the new coordinates
Translate a shape 3 units right and 2 units up and describe the movement
Explain that a reflected/translated shape is congruent to the original
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} slides or flips a shape on squared paper, can they describe exactly where it ends up and confirm the shape itself hasn't changed size or angles?

nodes.displayName: 长方形的角与边长关系
nodes.description: Use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles
evidence: Given one side of a rectangle is 8 cm and the perimeter is 28 cm, find the other side
Explain that all angles in a rectangle are 90°
Find a missing side of a rectangle given its area and one side length
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows one side of a rectangular garden is 7 m, can they tell you the length of the opposite side and all four corner angles — without measuring?

nodes.description: Understand that an angle is a geometric shape formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint (vertex); recognise angles in real-life contexts and 2-D shapes
evidence: Identify the vertex and arms of an angle in a diagram
Find examples of angles in the classroom (e.g. open door, clock hands)
Explain why two rays meeting at a point form an angle
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you draw two lines starting from the same point on paper, can {{name}} tell you that the space between them is an angle — and point to the vertex where they meet?

nodes.displayName: 平面图形 · 按尺寸和角度画图
nodes.description: Draw 2-D shapes using given dimensions and angles, using a ruler and protractor accurately
evidence: Draw a triangle with sides 5 cm, 7 cm and an included angle of 60°
Construct a rectangle with given length and width using a ruler and set square
Draw a regular pentagon given the side length and interior angle
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to draw a triangle with sides of 5 cm and 7 cm with a 40° angle between them, can they use a ruler and protractor to draw it accurately?

nodes.displayName: 立体图形 · 建立体与展开图
nodes.description: Recognise, describe, and build simple 3-D shapes, including making nets
evidence: Identify which net will fold into a given 3-D shape
Construct the net of a triangular prism and fold it to verify
Describe a 3-D shape by naming its faces, edges, and vertices
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a flat cross-shaped piece of card (a net), can they predict what 3-D shape it will make when folded up — and then fold it to check?

nodes.displayName: 三角形、四边形与正多边形的未知角
nodes.description: Find unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals, and regular polygons using angle sum properties
evidence: Find a missing angle in a triangle given two angles (using angle sum = 180°)
Calculate a missing angle in a quadrilateral (angle sum = 360°)
Calculate the interior angle of a regular hexagon from the angle sum formula
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows that angles in a triangle always add up to 180°, and two angles in a triangle are 55° and 70°, can they work out the third angle without measuring it?

nodes.description: Compare and classify geometric shapes based on their properties and sizes; understand that attributes belonging to a category also belong to all subcategories; classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
evidence: Explain why all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares
Place quadrilaterals in a hierarchy diagram showing subset relationships
Identify properties shared by all parallelograms and explain why rhombuses and rectangles are special cases
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If someone asks {{name}} "is a square also a rectangle?", can they explain why the answer is yes — because a square has all the properties of a rectangle plus equal sides?

nodes.displayName: 坐标 · 用负数描述位置
nodes.description: Describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants); use coordinates with negative values
evidence: Plot points with negative coordinates such as (−3, 4) and (2, −5) on a four-quadrant grid
Identify the quadrant in which a given point lies
Describe the position of a shape using coordinates in all four quadrants
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is playing a game where ships can be at negative coordinates too, can they correctly plot and read positions like (−3, 2) or (1, −4) on a grid?

nodes.description: Illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter, and circumference; know that the diameter is twice the radius
evidence: Label the radius, diameter, and circumference on a circle diagram
Calculate the diameter given a radius of 4.5 cm (diameter = 9 cm)
Explain the relationship between radius and diameter in their own words
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a round plate and a ruler, can they measure the diameter — and explain how the radius compares to the diameter?

nodes.sourceName: Plotting points in the first quadrant
nodes.description: Plot and read ordered pairs in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane; represent real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points and interpreting coordinate values in context
evidence: Plot the point (4, 7) accurately on a first-quadrant grid
Graph a set of data pairs (e.g. time vs distance) as points on the coordinate plane
Read coordinates of a plotted point and explain what they represent in a given scenario
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you tell {{name}} a car journey passes through grid points (2, 3), (5, 7), and (8, 4) on a map, can they plot those points and describe what the journey looks like?

nodes.description: Understand a coordinate system defined by two perpendicular number lines (axes) with an origin at (0,0); know that an ordered pair (x, y) specifies a unique point where the first number gives horizontal distance and the second gives vertical distance from the origin
evidence: Identify the x-axis, y-axis, and origin on a coordinate grid
Explain that (3, 5) means go 3 along the x-axis and 5 up the y-axis
Distinguish (2, 4) from (4, 2) by explaining each coordinate's meaning
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a map with a grid and you describe a location as "3 across and 5 up from the origin", can they find the exact point — and explain what each of the two numbers tells you?

nodes.description: Describe and perform translations, reflections and rotations of shapes with dynamic geometry software where appropriate as well as by hand, recognise what changes (position, orientation) and what stays the same (side lengths, angles, shape and size), and identify symmetries in the resulting figures
evidence: Use dynamic geometry software to translate a triangle 3 units right and 2 units up, reflect it in a vertical line and rotate it 90 degrees about a vertex
Measure the original and each image in the software and state that side lengths and angles stay the same while position, and for reflections and rotations orientation, change
Identify the line and rotational symmetry of a design made by reflecting and rotating one shape
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses a drawing app to flip, slide or turn a shape, can they explain what changed (where it is, which way it faces) and what stayed the same (its size and angles)?

nodes.description: Draw and translate simple shapes on the coordinate plane; reflect shapes in the axes
evidence: Translate a triangle 3 units right and 2 units down on a coordinate grid and state the new coordinates
Reflect a shape in the x-axis and list the coordinates of the reflected vertices
Explain how translation changes coordinates (add/subtract) while reflection changes the sign of one coordinate
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a triangle at coordinates (1, 2), (3, 2), and (2, 4) on a grid, can they then reflect it across the x-axis and tell you the new coordinates of each corner?

nodes.displayName: 理解角 · 交点、直线与对顶角
nodes.description: Recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite; find missing angles using these properties
evidence: Find a missing angle at a point given the other angles (total 360°)
Use the straight-line property (angles sum to 180°) to find an unknown angle
Identify vertically opposite angles and use the property that they are equal to find unknowns
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If two straight lines cross each other, can {{name}} tell you which pairs of angles are equal (vertically opposite) — and find a missing angle if you give them one of the others?

nodes.displayName: 立体图形 · 面、棱、顶点与截面
nodes.description: Use the properties of faces, surfaces, edges, and vertices of 3-D shapes (cubes, cuboids, prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres) to solve problems, including visualising cross-sections
evidence: Count and describe the faces, edges, and vertices of a triangular prism and a square-based pyramid
Describe the 2-D cross-section produced by slicing a cylinder horizontally or a cone vertically
Use properties of 3-D shapes to determine whether a given net will fold into a specified solid
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} slices a cylinder straight across the middle like cutting a tin of beans in half, can they describe the shape of the cut surface? What about slicing at an angle?

nodes.sourceTitle: 三角形与多边形的内角和
nodes.sourceName: Angle sums in triangles and polygons
nodes.displayName: 三角形与多边形的内角和
nodes.description: Derive and use the angle sum in a triangle (180°), use it to deduce the angle sum in any polygon ((n−2) × 180°), and calculate interior and exterior angles of regular polygons
evidence: Calculate a missing angle in a triangle by subtracting the known angles from 180°
Find the sum of interior angles in a hexagon by dividing it into triangles
Calculate each interior and exterior angle of a regular polygon given the number of sides
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows two angles of a triangle are 50° and 70°, can they work out the third? And can they figure out the angles inside a regular pentagon?

nodes.description: Derive and apply formulae for the area of triangles, parallelograms, and trapezia, and for the volume of cuboids and other prisms (including cylinders), connecting each formula to its geometric reasoning
evidence: Calculate the area of a trapezium using A = ½(a + b) × h and explain why the formula works
Find the volume of a triangular prism by calculating cross-sectional area × length
Derive the formula for the volume of a cylinder as π × r² × h by reasoning from the prism formula
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to tile a triangular section of a patio with a base of 4 m and height of 3 m, can they work out the area to know how many tiles to buy?

nodes.description: Identify properties of translations, rotations, and reflections; describe and perform these transformations on given figures, and understand that the image is congruent to the original
evidence: Reflect a shape in a given mirror line (including diagonal lines) and state the coordinates of the image
Rotate a shape about a given centre by 90° or 180° and describe the result
Translate a shape by a given vector and verify that lengths and angles are preserved
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to rotate a triangle 90° clockwise around a fixed point, can they work out where each corner ends up — and confirm the triangle is still the same size and shape?

nodes.description: Compare the parallel cross-sections of objects and recognise that slices of a right prism taken parallel to its end (base) faces are all congruent to those faces, while parallel slices of pyramids and cones change in size
evidence: Slice a play-dough triangular prism parallel to its triangular end faces and show every slice is congruent to the end face
Explain why slices of a square pyramid taken parallel to its base get smaller towards the apex
Identify which of an unsharpened hexagonal pencil, a cone and a cereal box give congruent slices when cut parallel to their end faces
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} cuts slices off a rectangular block of cheese, parallel to its end, can they explain why every slice is the same rectangle as the end — but slices of an ice-cream cone would keep getting smaller?

nodes.description: Draw and measure line segments and angles accurately, and construct triangles from given conditions using the drawing approaches the standard calls for: ruler and protractor for two sides and the included angle (SAS) or two angles and the included side (ASA); ruler and compasses for three sides (SSS), using intersecting arcs; and dynamic geometry software; check each construction by measuring the remaining sides and angles (to within about 1 mm and 1°). Interpreting scale drawings is covered in Scale drawings and maps; deciding whether conditions give one, many or no triangles is covered in Which triangles are possible
evidence: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, angle A = 40° and AC = 5 cm using a ruler and protractor, then measure BC and the other two angles
Construct a triangle with sides 6 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm using a ruler and compasses, drawing intersecting arcs from each end of the 6 cm base

Construct a triangle with angles of 50° and 60° at the ends of a 7 cm side in dynamic geometry software, measure the third angle (70°), and drag the vertices to show that the triangle can move or rotate but cannot change its shape or size while those ASA conditions hold
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to draw a triangle with sides of 7 cm and 5 cm and a 40° angle between them, could they draw it accurately with a ruler and protractor — and then measure the third side to check?

nodes.description: Use conventional geometric terms and notation to describe, sketch, and draw points, lines, parallel and perpendicular lines, right angles, regular polygons, and reflectively/rotationally symmetric polygons
evidence: Use correct notation for line segments (AB), angles (∠ABC), and parallel lines (AB ∥ CD)
Sketch a regular hexagon and describe its rotational and reflective symmetry
Identify and label perpendicular and parallel lines in a given figure using standard symbols
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to describe a triangle using proper geometry notation — naming its angles and sides with letters — can they do it clearly enough for someone else to draw it?

nodes.sourceTitle: 三角形与四边形的特征
nodes.displayName: 三角形、四边形与圆的特征
nodes.description: Derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, and circles using appropriate language, including interior angles, diagonals, symmetry, and relationships between side lengths
evidence: List and verify properties of a parallelogram (opposite sides parallel/equal, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other)
Explain why a square is a special case of both a rectangle and a rhombus
Derive the relationship between the radius, diameter, and circumference of a circle
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} why the diagonals of a rectangle are always equal in length, can they explain it using the properties of the shape — rather than just measuring to check?

nodes.description: Draw polygons in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane from given vertex coordinates; find the length of a horizontal or vertical side from the coordinates of its endpoints (which share an x- or a y-coordinate) by subtracting when both endpoints lie on the same side of the axis, and by adding their distances from the axis (absolute values) when the side crosses it; and use these lengths to find perimeters, areas, missing vertices and distances in real-world and mathematical problems such as maps and plans
evidence: Plot (−3, 2), (4, 2), (4, −1) and (−3, −1), join them to form a rectangle, and find its side lengths (7 and 3 units), perimeter (20 units) and area (21 square units)
Explain that (−5, 6) to (−5, 1) is 6 − 1 = 5 units, while (2, −4) to (2, 3) is |−4| + |3| = 7 units because that side crosses the x-axis
Find how far the library at (−6, 3) is from the park at (2, 3) on a town map where each grid unit is 100 m (800 m)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} plots the corners of a vegetable patch at (−3, 2), (4, 2), (4, −1) and (−3, −1) on a grid where each square is 1 metre, could they draw it and work out how long each side is, even where the patch crosses the axes?

nodes.description: Recognise and use combinations of translations, reflections and rotations to create tessellations and other geometric patterns, using dynamic geometry software where appropriate
evidence: Explain why equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons tessellate but regular pentagons do not
Create a tessellation from a modified tile by translating and rotating it, describing the transformations used
Use geometry software to build a frieze pattern by repeatedly reflecting and translating a motif
nodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} looks at bathroom tiles or a brick wall, can they explain why the shapes fit together with no gaps — and create their own tiling pattern by sliding, flipping or turning a shape?

nodes.displayName: 理解角 · 用角的关系解决多步问题
nodes.description: Apply the properties of angles at a point (360°), on a straight line (180°), and vertically opposite angles to find unknown angles in multi-step problems
evidence: Find a missing angle using the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180°
Use vertically opposite angles are equal to set up and solve an equation for an unknown
Combine multiple angle facts in a single diagram to find several missing angles step by step
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a diagram with several angles marked at crossing lines and some unknown, can they use the rules about straight lines and crossing lines to find all the missing angles step by step?

nameReview.qualifier: 用角的关系解决多步问题

nodes.description: Understand and use the relationship between parallel lines cut by a transversal: corresponding angles, alternate interior angles, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles; use these to find unknown angles
evidence: Identify alternate, corresponding, and co-interior angle pairs in a diagram with parallel lines
Explain why alternate angles are equal using the concept of translation along the transversal
Find missing angles in a parallel-line diagram using a combination of angle relationships
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a Z-shape or F-shape formed by two parallel lines and a crossing line in a diagram, can they identify the equal angles and explain why they’re equal?

nodes.description: Calculate the circumference and area of circles using the formulae C = πd (or 2πr) and A = πr², and solve problems involving perimeters and areas of composite shapes that include circular parts
evidence: Calculate the circumference and area of a circle given its radius or diameter
Find the perimeter or area of a composite shape made from rectangles and semicircles
Explain the relationship between π, diameter, and circumference informally
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to know how far a bicycle wheel travels in one full rotation, can they use the diameter of the wheel and π (pi) to work out the circumference?

nodes.description: Know and use the criteria for triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS), use standard labelling conventions for sides and angles of triangle ABC, and determine whether two triangles are congruent
evidence: State which congruence criterion (SSS, SAS, ASA, or RHS) applies to a given pair of triangles
Use the notation △ABC ≅ △DEF and match corresponding sides and angles
Use two non-congruent triangles that share two sides and a non-included angle to explain why SSA is not a congruence criterion
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown two triangles where all three sides of one match all three sides of the other, can they explain why those triangles must be identical in shape and size?

nodes.description: Use ruler and compasses to perform standard constructions: perpendicular bisector of a line segment, perpendicular to a line from or at a given point, and bisecting an angle
evidence: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment using compasses and a straight edge
Construct an angle bisector and verify by measuring both halves
Construct a perpendicular from a point to a line using compasses only
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has only a ruler and a pair of compasses, can they construct a line that cuts another line segment exactly in half at a right angle — without using a protractor?

nodes.description: Understand similarity as a relationship where one shape is an enlargement of another; construct similar shapes by enlargement with a given scale factor and centre, with and without coordinate grids
evidence: Enlarge a shape by a given scale factor from a specified centre of enlargement
Determine the scale factor between two similar shapes by comparing corresponding sides
Explain why corresponding angles in similar shapes are equal while sides are in proportion
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to enlarge a photo so it's three times bigger, can they work out the new dimensions — and explain that the shape stays the same but all lengths increase by the same factor?

nodes.sourceTitle: 立体图形的表面积与体积
nodes.sourceName: Surface area and volume of solids
nodes.displayName: 立体图形的表面积与体积
nodes.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the surface area and volume of right prisms (including triangular and trapezoidal prisms) and of solids composed of cubes and right prisms: find a prism's surface area as the two bases plus the rectangular side faces; find volume as base area × height, including bases that are composite polygons; for composite solids, add the volumes of the parts but find the surface area from the exposed faces only, subtracting the areas hidden where parts join; and decide whether a problem needs area, surface area or volume
evidence: Find the surface area of a triangular prism 10 cm long with right-triangle ends (sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm) as 2 × 6 + (3 + 4 + 5) × 10 = 132 cm²
Find the volume (40 cm³) and surface area (80 cm², not 88 cm²) of a 2 cm cube glued on top of a 4 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm block, removing the two 4 cm² faces hidden where they join
Find the soil for a planter 0.5 m deep whose L-shaped base is a 3 m × 1 m and a 2 m × 1.5 m rectangle (6 m² × 0.5 m = 3 m³), and explain why painting its outside walls needs surface area instead
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} built a model from two boxes glued together, could they work out how much space it takes up and how much paint would cover its outside — remembering not to paint the faces that are glued together?

nodes.sourceTitle: 哪些边长能组成三角形
nodes.displayName: 根据边角条件判断三角形能否作出
nodes.description: Decide whether given side and angle conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle, and explain why, predicting with a freehand sketch and testing by construction (ruler and protractor, compasses, or dynamic geometry software): three sides give exactly one triangle when each pair of sides adds to more than the third, and none otherwise — if the two shorter sides add to less than the longest, the construction arcs do not meet, and if they add to exactly the longest (e.g. 3, 4 and 7), the arcs touch only on the base line, so the sides lie flat in a straight line rather than forming a triangle; three angles must add to 180° and then fix only the shape, not the size, so many triangles fit (none if the sum is not 180°); two sides with the included angle, or two angles with the included side, give exactly one triangle; and two sides with an angle that is not between them can give two, one or no triangles
evidence: Show that sides of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm make no triangle (the arcs do not meet) and that 3 cm, 4 cm and 7 cm make none either (the arcs touch on the base, giving a straight line), while 3 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm make exactly one
Explain that angles of 50°, 60° and 70° fit many triangles of different sizes, while angles of 100°, 50° and 40° fit none because they add to 190°
Sketch freehand, then construct, two different triangles with AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm and angle A = 40°, and explain why making the 40° angle the one between the two sides gives only one triangle
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to make a triangle from straws 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm long, could they predict that it can't be done and explain why — and say why 'angles of 50°, 60° and 70°' could describe lots of different-sized triangles?

nodes.description: Apply Pythagoras’ Theorem (a² + b² = c²) to calculate unknown side lengths in right-angled triangles, including in real-world and coordinate-geometry contexts
evidence: Calculate the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle given the two shorter sides
Find a shorter side given the hypotenuse and the other short side
Use Pythagoras’ Theorem to find the distance between two points on a coordinate grid
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to check whether a shelf bracket makes a perfect right angle and the sides measure 30 cm, 40 cm, and 50 cm, can they use Pythagoras to verify?

nodes.description: Use the trigonometric ratios sin, cos, and tan in right-angled triangles to find unknown sides and angles, including setting up the correct ratio for a given problem
evidence: Identify which trigonometric ratio to use (SOH CAH TOA) based on the known and unknown sides
Calculate an unknown side using sin, cos, or tan and a known angle
Find an unknown angle using the inverse trigonometric function (e.g. tan⁻¹)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a ladder is 5 metres long and leans against a wall at 70° to the ground, can they use trigonometry to work out how high up the wall it reaches?

nodes.description: Compare and describe capacity and volume using language such as full, empty, more than, less than, half full
evidence: Compare two containers and say which holds more/less
Use 'half full' and 'quarter full' to describe a container
Solve practical problems like 'Which cup has more water?'
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has two cups of different sizes, can they tell you which holds more water — and describe one as "more full" or "less full" than the other?

nodes.description: Use comparative language for time: quicker, slower, earlier, later
evidence: Compare two events and say which was quicker/slower
Use 'earlier' and 'later' correctly to describe daily events
Solve practical problems like 'Who finished first?'
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} finishes their dinner before a sibling, can they tell you who finished earlier — and which one was quicker?

nodes.description: Compare two objects directly by length or height and describe the difference using language such as long, short, tall, longer, shorter, taller, double, half
evidence: Stand two children back-to-back and say who is taller/shorter
Directly compare the heights of two towers and describe one as taller
Use 'longer' and 'shorter' to compare two ribbons placed side by side
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stands next to the kitchen table and the front door, can they tell you which is taller — and whether they themselves are shorter or taller than each one?

nodes.sourceTitle: 物体有哪些可测量的量
nodes.displayName: 物体有哪些可测量的量
nodes.description: Describe and identify measurable attributes of objects such as length, height, weight, and capacity; use comparative language (longer, shorter, heavier, lighter, more, less)
evidence: Identify that a pencil has length and can be measured
Describe multiple attributes of one object (e.g. a bottle has height, weight, and capacity)
Use words like 'long', 'heavy', 'full' to describe objects

nodes.displayName: 测量质量与重量 · 直接比较轻重
nodes.description: Compare two objects directly by mass or weight and describe the difference using language such as heavy, light, heavier than, lighter than
evidence: Heft two objects and say which is heavier/lighter
Use a simple balance to compare the weight of two objects
Describe one object as 'heavier than' another
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} holds a bag of apples in one hand and a feather in the other, can they tell you which is heavier and use words like "much heavier than" to describe the difference?

nodes.description: Sequence events in chronological order using language such as before, after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon, evening
evidence: Order three daily events using 'first', 'next', 'last'
Use 'yesterday', 'today', 'tomorrow' correctly
Describe an event as happening in the 'morning' or 'afternoon'
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to describe what happened this morning in order, can they use words like "first", "then", "after that" — putting breakfast before leaving for school?

nodes.description: Measure and begin to record capacity and volume using non-standard and standard units

Begin to use litres as a unit of capacity
Record capacity measurements with a number and unit
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} fills a jug using a small cup, can they count how many cups it takes — and understand that this tells you how much the jug holds?

nodes.description: Recognise and know the value of different coins and notes
evidence: Identify 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2 coins
Know that a £2 coin is worth more than a 50p coin
Recognise £5 and £10 notes
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a handful of coins, can they name each one — like 2p, 5p, 20p — and sort them from least to most valuable?

nodes.description: Recognise and use language relating to dates, including days of the week, weeks, months, and years
evidence: Name the seven days of the week in order
Name the twelve months of the year in order
Understand that a year is made up of months and weeks
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} what day it is today, what day yesterday was, and what month we're in, can they answer all three — and tell you how many months are in a year?

nodes.description: Measure and begin to record time in hours, minutes, and seconds
evidence: Use a sand timer or stopwatch to time an activity
Begin to understand that 1 minute = 60 seconds
Record a duration in simple terms (e.g. 'it took about 2 minutes')
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches the second hand go all the way round a clock, can they count that as one minute — and estimate roughly how many minutes their favourite TV show lasts?

nodes.description: Measure and begin to record lengths and heights using non-standard and standard units
evidence: Measure the length of a table using cubes and record the result
Begin to use a ruler to measure in centimetres
Record a measurement as a number with a unit
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the length of a book using small cubes laid end to end, can they count how many cubes it takes — and then try measuring the same book with a ruler?

nodes.displayName: 测量质量与重量 · 用单位测量质量
nodes.description: Measure and begin to record mass/weight using non-standard and standard units
evidence: Use a balance to compare masses of two objects
Measure mass using non-standard units (e.g. 'this book weighs 5 cubes')
Begin to read a simple scale for mass
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses balance scales to compare two objects, can they tell you which is heavier — and if given weights like 100g, can they balance an object on the scale?

nodes.sourceName: Telling Time: Hours and Half Hours
nodes.description: Tell and write the time to the hour and half past the hour on analogue clocks and digital displays (e.g. 3 o'clock = 3:00, half past 7 = 7:30), and draw clock hands to show these times, placing the hour hand halfway between two numbers for half past

Write half past 7 as 7:30 and match the digital times 3:00 and 7:30 to the right analogue clocks
Draw the hands on a blank clock face for half past 2, with the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand halfway between 2 and 3
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you point to a clock showing 3 o'clock or half past two, can {{name}} tell you the time, say which digital time (3:00 or 2:30) matches it — and draw hands on a blank clock face to show a time you call out?

nodes.displayName: 用不同硬币凑成相同金额
