nodes.description: Represent and order numbers to at least 1000 using physical base-ten blocks and virtual materials (on-screen base-ten blocks and interactive number lines), connecting each representation to the numeral
evidence: Build 347 with real base-ten blocks and again with on-screen base-ten blocks and say how many hundreds, tens and ones
Drag 608, 680, 86 and 860 onto an on-screen 0-1000 number line in order
Show on screen that 10 hundreds blocks make 1000 and write the numeral
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses a maths app with hundreds, tens and ones blocks, can they build 347 on screen and with real blocks — and put 608, 680 and 860 in order on a number line?

nodes.description: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members
evidence: Pair objects and determine whether there is one left over (odd) or not (even)
Count a group by 2s to determine if the total is even
Write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends (e.g. 8 = 4 + 4)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a group of 14 objects, can they tell you whether that number is odd or even — for example by pairing them up to see if any are left over?

nodes.description: Compare and order numbers up to 1000 using >, =, and < symbols, based on place-value understanding
evidence: Compare two three-digit numbers by examining hundreds first, then tens, then ones
Use >, =, and < correctly to record comparisons of three-digit numbers
Order a set of numbers up to 1000 from smallest to largest
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a set of three-digit numbers like 456, 231, and 789, can they put them in order and use > and < correctly?

nodes.description: Solve number problems and practical problems involving place value of numbers up to 1000
evidence: Solve a problem that requires identifying how many hundreds, tens, or ones are in a number
Apply place-value knowledge to a practical context (e.g. counting money in pounds)
Explain the strategy used to solve a place-value problem
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told 'I have 4 hundreds, 3 tens, and 7 ones — what number is that?', can they put it together and tell you 437?

nodes.description: Read and write numbers to 1000 in numerals, number names, and expanded form
evidence: Read a three-digit numeral aloud correctly
Write a three-digit number in words (e.g. 'three hundred and forty-two')
Write a number in expanded form (e.g. 600 + 30 + 7)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 1,000 — both as numerals and in words — like reading '642' as 'six hundred and forty-two'?

nodes.description: Identify, represent and estimate three-digit numbers using different representations: place a number on a 0–1000 number line marked only in hundreds or unmarked, estimate the value of a marked point, and represent a number with base-ten blocks (hundreds, tens and ones), a place-value chart and a drawing, including numbers with a zero digit and non-standard partitions
evidence: Mark 346 in about the right place on a 0–1000 number line marked in hundreds (between 300 and 400, a little before halfway), and estimate that an unlabelled point three-quarters of the way along is about 750
Represent 507 with base-ten blocks and on a place-value chart, showing the empty tens column as 0
Match a drawing of 3 hundreds, 14 tens and 2 ones to the numeral 442
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a number line from 0 to 1000 marked only in hundreds, can they point to roughly where 346 goes — and show 346 another way, such as hundreds, tens and ones blocks or a place-value chart?

nodes.description: Understand that the multiples of 100 (100–900) each represent a number of hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones
evidence: Identify that 300 means 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones
Place multiples of 100 on a number line to 1000
Read and write multiples of 100 and explain their place-value structure
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that 700 means 7 hundreds with no tens and no ones — and show what that looks like using base-ten blocks or a drawing?

nodes.sourceName: The three digits of a three-digit number
nodes.description: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones
evidence: State the value of each digit in a three-digit number (e.g. in 362, the 3 represents 3 hundreds)
Partition a three-digit number into hundreds, tens, and ones (e.g. 485 = 400 + 80 + 5)
Explain why 706 has 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the number 348, can they tell you there are 3 hundreds, 4 tens, and 8 ones — rather than just reading the digits as 'three four eight'?

nodes.description: Find 1000 more or less than a given number
evidence: Given 4,562, state that 1000 more is 5,562 and 1000 less is 3,562
Explain using place value that only the thousands digit changes
Apply this skill to numbers beyond 10,000
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '1,000 more than 3,456' or '1,000 less than 7,200' in their head — knowing only the thousands digit changes?

nodes.description: Order and compare numbers beyond 1000
evidence: Compare two four-digit numbers using >, <, and = by examining digits from the highest place value
Order a set of numbers up to 10,000 from smallest to largest
Justify the ordering using place-value reasoning
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} put a set of four-digit numbers like 4,321, 1,876, and 9,045 in order from smallest to largest — comparing them digit by digit?

nodes.description: Count backwards through zero to include negative numbers
evidence: Count backwards from 5 through zero: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 …
Place negative numbers on a number line
Understand that negative numbers are less than zero and use them in context (e.g. temperature)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count backwards past zero into negative numbers — like 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −3 — without hesitating at zero?

nodes.description: Identify, represent, and estimate numbers up to 10,000 using different representations
evidence: Represent a four-digit number on a place-value chart or with base-ten materials
Estimate where a number falls on a 0–10,000 number line
Match different representations of the same number (e.g. expanded form, place-value counters, numeral)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} mark a number like 6,400 roughly in the right place on a number line that goes from 0 to 10,000 — and explain how they decided where to put it?

nodes.description: Recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)
evidence: State the value of each digit in a four-digit number (e.g. in 7,345 the 7 represents 7 thousands)
Partition a four-digit number into thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones
Compose a four-digit number from given place-value parts (e.g. 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the number 5,347, can they tell you the value of each digit — that the 5 means 5,000, the 3 means 300, the 4 means 40, and the 7 means 7?

nodes.description: Solve number and practical problems involving place value with increasingly large positive numbers
evidence: Solve a problem requiring rounding, comparing, or ordering numbers beyond 1000
Apply place-value knowledge in a practical context (e.g. population figures, distances)
Explain the strategy used, referencing place-value understanding
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked 'what is the largest 4-digit even number you can make from the digits 3, 7, 1, and 8?', can they work through it systematically and give you an answer?

nodes.displayName: 数的读写 · 整数的读写比较
nodes.description: Read, write, order, and compare whole numbers up to at least 1,000,000 using base-ten numerals, number names, expanded form, and place-value understanding
evidence: Write 403,072 in words and in expanded form
Compare 548,301 and 543,801 using < and explain the reasoning
Order four six-digit numbers from smallest to largest
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write numbers into the millions — like 1,340,000 — and put a set of large numbers in order correctly?

nodes.description: Read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and understand that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value
evidence: Read and write Roman numerals I, V, X, L, C and combinations up to 100
Convert between Roman numerals and Hindu-Arabic numerals (e.g. XLIV = 44)
Explain that Roman numerals have no zero and no place-value system
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like XIV (14) or XLII (42) — and do they know why we stopped using Roman numerals for most things once zero and place value were invented?

nodes.sourceTitle: 取整十、整百、整千的近似数
nodes.displayName: 取整十、整百、整千的近似数
nodes.description: Round any number to the nearest 10, 100, or 1000
evidence: Explain the rounding rule using a number line (which multiple is closer)
Apply rounding to estimate calculations
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a number like 4,738 to the nearest 10 (4,740), 100 (4,700), or 1,000 (5,000) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

nodes.displayName: 顺着数与倒着数 · 按10的幂走
nodes.description: Count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10, 100, 1000, 10,000, 100,000) for any given number up to 1,000,000
evidence: Count on in 10,000s from 462,000
Count back in 100,000s from 800,000
Identify the next three terms: 375,000; 475,000; 575,000; ...
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count forwards and backwards in steps of 1,000 or 10,000 from any starting number — like 34,500, 44,500, 54,500 — without losing track?

nodes.description: Interpret negative numbers in context (temperature, sea level, bank balance); count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero
evidence: Place –3, –1, 0, 2, 5 on a number line
The temperature is –4°C and rises by 7 degrees — what is the new temperature?
Count backwards from 3 in ones: 3, 2, 1, 0, –1, –2
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If the temperature drops to −5°C overnight and rises to 3°C by day, can {{name}} place both on a number line and say how many degrees warmer the daytime temperature is?

nodes.description: Recognise that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (e.g. 700 ÷ 70 = 10)
evidence: Explain that the 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300
Complete: 700 ÷ 70 = __ and explain using place-value reasoning
State how many times greater the value of the 5 in 50,000 is than the 5 in 5,000
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that in 700, the 7 is worth 10 times more than in 70 — because moving one place to the left multiplies the value by 10?

nodes.description: Read Roman numerals to 1000 (M) and recognise years written in Roman numerals
evidence: Read MCMXCIX as 1999
Write 2024 in Roman numerals (MMXXIV)
Explain the subtractive principle: IV = 4 not IIII
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like MMXIX (2019) or CDXLIV (444) — and recognise the year a film or building was made when it's shown in Roman numerals?

nodes.description: Round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, or 100,000 using place-value understanding
evidence: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000 (460,000)
Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000 and explain the boundary case
Use rounding to estimate the sum of 387,412 + 214,560
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a large number like 346,712 to the nearest 1,000 (347,000) or 10,000 (350,000) — identifying which digit to look at for each rounding?

nodes.description: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000
evidence: What is the largest six-digit number with digits summing to 15?
A stadium holds 67,450 people. Round to the nearest thousand for a news report
Order the populations of five cities and find the difference between the largest and smallest
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told the population of a city is 2,347,819, can they read that number aloud correctly and say roughly how many millions it is?

nodes.description: Round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy
evidence: Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places (3.46)
Use rounding to estimate 4.83 × 2.17 ≈ 5 × 2 = 10
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a decimal like 3.748 to one decimal place (3.7) or two decimal places (3.75) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

nodes.displayName: 用正负数表示变化与跨零差值
nodes.description: Use negative numbers in context (temperature, finance, sea level); calculate intervals across zero
evidence: The temperature falls from 3°C to −5°C — what is the drop? (8 degrees)
Calculate the difference between a bank balance of −£120 and £350
Order −7, −3, 0, 2, 5 on a number line and find the interval from −7 to 5
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a bank account goes from −£45 to +£120, can {{name}} work out the total change — counting through zero to get £165?

nodes.description: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding, and negative numbers up to 10,000,000
evidence: A country's population is 8,274,500 — round to the nearest million for a headline
Order the depths of three ocean trenches given in metres including negative values
Estimate the total attendance at three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that the distance to the Moon is about 384,400 km, can they round it to the nearest 10,000 km and say whether it's closer to 380,000 or 390,000?

nodes.description: Explain patterns in zeros when multiplying by powers of 10 and in decimal-point placement when multiplying/dividing by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10 (e.g. 10³ = 1000)
evidence: Write 10⁴ = 10,000 and explain the exponent means four factors of 10
Explain why 3.4 × 10² = 340 by describing the decimal shift
Predict 2.56 × 10³ without calculating and explain the pattern
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why 10² = 100 and 10³ = 1,000, and why multiplying by 10 just adds a zero — connecting the pattern of zeros to place value?

nodes.description: Recognise that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left
evidence: Explain that the 4 in 0.04 is 1/10 of the 4 in 0.4
State that a digit moving one place left is ×10 and one place right is ÷10
Compare the value of the 6 in 6,000 and in 0.006
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that in 4.56, the digit 5 is worth 5 tenths — ten times less than the 5 in 54, and ten times more than the 5 in 0.056?

nodes.displayName: 数的读写 · 小数的读写比较
nodes.description: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form; compare using >, =, < based on place-value meaning
evidence: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 using place-value reasoning
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as 5.062
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write decimals like 3.047 or 0.625, say what each digit means (3 ones, 0 tenths, 4 hundredths, 7 thousandths), and put a set of decimals in order?

nodes.description: Read, write, order, and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit
evidence: Write 4,302,561 in words
Order four seven-digit numbers from smallest to largest
State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200 as seven million
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 10 million — like 4,302,617 — and say the value of any digit in the number?

nodes.description: Identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (e.g. in 4.378, the 7 represents 7 hundredths)
evidence: State the value of each digit in 2.635 (2 ones, 6 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths)
Explain the relationship between adjacent decimal places (each place is ten times smaller)
Write a number given digit values (e.g. 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: In the number 4.378, can {{name}} tell you that the 7 represents 7 hundredths — not 7 tenths or 7 thousandths?

nodes.description: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from zero on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude in real-world contexts; distinguish absolute value comparisons from ordering statements
evidence: Define absolute value as distance from zero on a number line
Calculate the absolute value of positive and negative rational numbers
Distinguish between comparing absolute values and comparing signed numbers in real-world contexts
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you that the absolute value of −7 is 7 — because it's 7 steps from zero on a number line regardless of direction — and use this idea to compare distances?

nodes.description: Round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy including to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures
evidence: Round numbers to a given number of decimal places
Round numbers to a given number of significant figures
Choose an appropriate degree of accuracy for a given context
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a measurement like 12.3746 km to 2 decimal places (12.37 km) or 3 significant figures (12.4 km) — and explain when each level of precision is appropriate?

nodes.displayName: 在数轴上表示正负数、小数与分数
nodes.description: Understand and use place value for decimals, measures, and integers of any size; extend the number system to include all positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a single number line
evidence: Identify the value of any digit in numbers of any size including decimals
Place positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line
Use place value to compare and order numbers across the full number system
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} place a mix of numbers — like 3, −2, 0.5, −1.75, and ¼ — all on the same number line, in the right order?

nodes.displayName: 比较正负数、分数与小数
nodes.description: Order positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line; use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values including negative numbers and mixed representations
evidence: Order a mixed set of positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions
Use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ correctly in mathematical statements
Compare numbers presented in different forms such as 0.75 and 3/4
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a mixed list like 2.5, −3, ¾, 0, and −0.5, can they put them in order from least to greatest using a number line if needed?

nodes.displayName: 整数幂与平方根、立方根
nodes.description: Use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube, and higher); recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, and 5; distinguish between exact representations of roots and their decimal approximations
evidence: Calculate squares, cubes, and higher integer powers of whole numbers
Find square roots and cube roots of perfect squares and perfect cubes
Recognise key powers (powers of 2 up to 2¹⁰, powers of 3 up to 3⁵, etc.) and distinguish exact roots from approximations
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out that √25 = 5 and ∛27 = 3 — knowing these are the inverse of squaring and cubing — and say whether √50 is closer to 7 or 8?

nodes.displayName: 四舍五入的误差与上下界
nodes.description: Use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible resulting errors expressed using inequality notation a < x ≤ b; understand upper and lower bounds of rounded values
evidence: Estimate the answer to a calculation by rounding all values appropriately
Calculate upper and lower bounds of a rounded measurement
Express error intervals using inequality notation
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a length is measured as 7 cm to the nearest cm, can {{name}} say the actual length could be anywhere from 6.5 cm to 7.5 cm — understanding that rounding creates a range of possible values?

nodes.displayName: 科学记数法与10的整数次幂
nodes.description: Interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer; convert between ordinary numbers and standard form
evidence: Convert large and small numbers into standard form A × 10ⁿ
Convert numbers from standard form back to ordinary notation
Compare and order numbers given in standard form
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write 3,400,000 as 3.4 × 10⁶ and convert back — understanding that standard form is a shorthand for very large or very small numbers?

nodes.description: Appreciate the infinite nature of the sets of integers, real numbers, and rational numbers; position integers on a number line and distinguish between rational and irrational numbers
evidence: Explain that rational numbers can be written as a fraction of two integers and have terminating or repeating decimals
Give examples of irrational numbers and explain why their decimal expansions neither terminate nor repeat
Appreciate that between any two numbers there are infinitely many other numbers
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that numbers like √2 and π can't be written as exact fractions — and that their decimal expansions go on forever without repeating?

nodes.description: Use probability language to describe and compare the likelihood of everyday events using words such as certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible
evidence: Place five everyday events (e.g. 'the sun will rise tomorrow', 'it will snow in July', 'I'll flip heads') on a scale from impossible to certain
Use 'likely', 'unlikely', 'certain', 'impossible', and 'even chance' correctly to describe different events
Explain why pulling a red ball from a bag of mostly red balls is 'likely' but not 'certain'
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} use words like "certain," "likely," "unlikely," and "impossible" correctly — for example, knowing that rolling a 7 on a normal die is impossible but rolling an even number is likely?

nodes.description: Conduct simple probability experiments — flipping a coin, rolling a die, pulling coloured counters from a bag — record results, and compare experimental outcomes with expected theoretical outcomes
evidence: Flip a coin 20 times, record heads and tails in a tally chart, and describe what they notice about the results
Roll a die 30 times and compare how often each number came up with what they expected
Pull counters from a bag, record results, and explain whether the outcomes matched their prediction
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} ever done an experiment like flipping a coin or rolling a die lots of times, recorded the results in a tally chart, and noticed any patterns in what came up?

nodes.description: Understand that 'equally likely' means every outcome has exactly the same chance of occurring; identify whether a given situation has equally likely outcomes (a fair coin, a fair die, a spinner with equal sections) or unequally likely outcomes (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with unequal sections)
evidence: Explain that a fair coin has equally likely outcomes because heads and tails each have the same chance
Identify whether a spinner with unequal sections has equally likely outcomes or not, and explain why
Give an example of a situation with equally likely outcomes and one without, explaining the difference
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell the difference between a fair situation — like rolling a normal die where every number has the same chance — and an unfair one, like a bag with many more of one colour than another?

nodes.description: Run repeated probability experiments and compare experimental (relative frequency) results with theoretical predictions; understand and demonstrate that as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends towards the theoretical probability — and that short runs can give very different results
evidence: Roll a die 60 times and compare experimental frequencies with the expected 10 per number
Explain why experimental results don't exactly match theoretical predictions but get closer with more trials
Predict what would happen if the experiment were repeated 600 times instead of 60
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} flips a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads, do they understand why this doesn't mean heads is "more likely" — and that the more times you flip, the closer the results get to 50:50?

nodes.sourceTitle: 独立与相互影响的事件
nodes.displayName: 独立与相互影响的事件
nodes.description: Identify whether events in chance experiments and everyday situations are independent (one does not affect the other) or dependent (the first outcome changes the chances of the next)
evidence: Explain that getting heads on one coin flip does not change the chance of heads on the next flip
Explain why taking a red marble out of a bag and not putting it back changes the chance of drawing red next
Sort five described pairs of events into independent and dependent
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} flips a coin and gets heads three times in a row, do they understand the next flip is still 50-50 — but that taking a lolly from a bag without putting it back does change what's left?

nodes.description: Compare the likelihood of different events and order them from least to most likely — including situations with unequal outcomes such as a bag with more of one colour than another, or a spinner with sections of different sizes — and explain reasoning using informal language
evidence: Order four or more events from least likely to most likely and justify each placement
Compare likelihoods when outcomes are not equally likely — e.g. 'Drawing red from a bag with 7 red and 3 blue is more likely than drawing blue'
Explain why some events are closer to 'even chance' and others are closer to 'certain' or 'impossible'
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a bag has 8 red counters and 2 blue ones, does {{name}} understand that picking red is much more likely than picking blue — and can they put different events in order from least to most likely?

nodes.description: Describe the probability of simple equally-likely outcomes using unit fractions: the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6, flipping heads is 1/2, picking one specific colour from three equally represented colours is 1/3; place these fractional probabilities on a 0-to-1 probability scale
evidence: State that the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6 and explain why
Express the probability of picking a red card from a standard deck as 26/52 or 1/2
Write the probability of a simple event as a fraction: favourable outcomes over total outcomes
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} flips a fair coin, do they know the probability of getting heads is 1/2 — and can they express similar simple probabilities as fractions and place them on a 0-to-1 scale?

nodes.description: Calculate the probability of a simple event with equally likely outcomes using the formula: probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes; express the result as a fraction in its simplest form; apply to rolling dice, drawing from bags, and other simple chance situations
evidence: Calculate the probability of drawing a blue marble from a bag of 3 blue and 7 red as 3/10
Use the formula P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes to solve at least three different problems
Explain why increasing the number of favourable outcomes increases the probability
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If there are 3 red and 7 blue balls in a bag, can {{name}} work out the probability of picking a red one and express it as a fraction in its simplest form?

nodes.description: Understand that when all possible outcomes of a trial are listed, their probabilities must add up to 1; use this to find the probability of an event NOT happening: P(not A) = 1 − P(A); apply this shortcut to avoid counting all unfavourable outcomes directly
evidence: List all outcomes of spinning a 4-colour spinner and verify their probabilities add up to 1
Calculate P(not rolling a 3) as 1 − 1/6 = 5/6 using the complement rule
Spot an error in a probability table where the values don't sum to 1 and explain what's wrong
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If the probability of it raining tomorrow is 0.3, can {{name}} work out the probability of it NOT raining — and explain why all probabilities in a situation must add up to 1?

nodes.description: Understand probability as a measure expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain); place events on the probability scale; express probabilities as fractions, decimals, and percentages
evidence: Place events on a number line from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), expressing positions as fractions or decimals
Explain that a probability of 0.5 means 'even chance' and connect this to the informal word 'likely'
Convert between informal language ('very unlikely') and a numerical position on the 0-to-1 scale
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write the same probability as a fraction, a decimal, and a percentage — for example, knowing that an even chance is ½, 0.5, and 50%?

nodes.description: Understand and apply the rule that probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes sum to one; use this to find the probability of a complementary event (P(not A) = 1 − P(A))
evidence: Verify that probabilities of all outcomes listed for a spinner sum to 1
Calculate the probability of NOT rolling a 6 as 1 − 1/6 = 5/6
Identify an error in a probability distribution where the values do not sum to 1
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a spinner has three sections and one has a probability of 0.4 and another has 0.35, can {{name}} work out the probability of landing on the third section without being told?

nodes.description: Record, describe, and analyse the frequency of outcomes from probability experiments to develop an understanding of relative frequency as an estimate of probability
evidence: Conduct a coin-toss experiment, record results in a frequency table, and calculate relative frequencies
Compare experimental results with theoretical probability and explain discrepancies
Predict that relative frequency approaches theoretical probability as the number of trials increases
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} rolls a die 60 times and records the results, can they compare how often each number came up with what they'd expect in theory — and explain why they might not match perfectly?

nodes.sourceTitle: 用数字工具模拟随机事件
nodes.displayName: 用数字工具模拟随机事件
nodes.description: Run chance simulations with an increasing number of trials using digital tools (spreadsheet random functions or online simulators), repeating each run size several times, and explain that relative frequencies tend to stabilise near the expected proportion as the number of trials grows, even though any single longer run need not be closer than a shorter one
evidence: Simulate runs of 10, 100 and 1000 dice rolls with a spreadsheet random-number function, repeating each run size 5 times, and record the proportion of 6s in every run
Plot the proportions for each run size and show that the 10-roll results spread widely while the 1000-roll results cluster near 1/6
Explain that results tend to settle near the expected 1/6 as trials increase, but a particular 1000-roll run can still be further from 1/6 than a lucky 10-roll run
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses a computer to 'roll a dice' 10 times, then 1000 times, and repeats each a few times, can they notice that the 1000-roll results bunch more closely around one-sixth sixes — while knowing any single run can still be a bit off?

nodes.description: Understand probability as a measure on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); use the language of probability including likely, unlikely, certain, and impossible
evidence: Place everyday events on a 0-to-1 probability scale with justification
Explain why a fair six-sided die gives each number a probability of 1/6
Distinguish between equally likely outcomes (fair coin) and unequally likely outcomes (biased spinner)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), place events on that scale as numbers, and tell you whether a game is fair or not?

nodes.description: Develop a probability model (a list of all the outcomes of a chance process with a probability for each, adding to 1) and use it to find probabilities of events: a uniform model gives every outcome the same probability (e.g. selecting a student at random from a class); a non-uniform model uses probabilities estimated from the observed frequencies of a chance process (e.g. how a tossed paper cup lands); compare a model's probabilities with observed frequencies and, when they disagree, explain whether the difference is plausibly chance variation or a sign that the model does not fit (e.g. a biased die or unequal spinner sections)
evidence: Use a uniform model to find that a randomly chosen student from a class of 25 with 12 girls is Jane with probability 1/25 and is a girl with probability 12/25
Toss a paper cup 50 times (e.g. 31 on its side, 13 open end up, 6 open end down), write a model with probabilities 0.62, 0.26 and 0.12, and explain why the three outcomes are not equally likely
Compare 600 rolls of a die that showed 160 sixes with the 100 sixes a fair-die model predicts, and argue that a difference this large suggests the die is biased rather than just chance
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} flips a paper cup 50 times and records whether it lands on its side, open end up or open end down, could they turn the results into a probability for each way of landing — and say whether the three are equally likely?

nodes.description: Enumerate sets and their unions and intersections systematically using tables, grids, and Venn diagrams to organise and count outcomes
evidence: List the elements in the union and intersection of two sets using a Venn diagram
Use a two-way table to enumerate all possible outcomes of two combined events
Shade regions of a Venn diagram to represent A ∪ B, A ∩ B, and A′ (complement)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use a table or Venn diagram to systematically list all the possible outcomes of two events — like rolling two dice — and use it to count favourable outcomes?

nodes.description: Design and use a simulation to estimate the probability of a compound event: choose a random device (coins, dice, spinners, counters drawn with replacement, random-digit tables, or calculator or software random numbers) and a mapping whose probabilities match the situation; define one complete trial (what is generated and when the trial stops) and the event being counted; run many trials; and estimate the probability as the event's relative frequency. Explain why the model fits (each simulated outcome has the same probability as the real one, and successive outcomes are independent when the real ones are), and why different runs give different estimates that become more consistent as the number of trials grows; where a theoretical value can be found (e.g. with a tree diagram), compare it with the estimate
evidence: Map random digits 0–3 to 'type A' and 4–9 to 'not type A' to model donors who are type A with probability 40%, and explain why the mapping fits (4 of the 10 equally likely digits)

Define one trial as reading digits until the first 0–3 appears, count it as a success if at least four digits were needed, run 50 trials and report the relative frequency as the estimated probability that at least four donors are needed
Explain why two groups who each ran 50 trials estimated 0.18 and 0.26, and why pooling their trials (or running 500) gives a more reliable estimate
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If 40% of blood donors are type A, could {{name}} use random numbers or a spinner to act out lots of donor queues, estimate how often at least four donors are needed before the first type A — and explain why doing it again gives a slightly different answer?

nodes.description: Generate theoretical sample spaces for single and combined events using listing, tables, and tree diagrams, and calculate theoretical probabilities as the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes
evidence: List all 36 outcomes when rolling two dice and find P(total = 7)
Draw a tree diagram for two successive events and multiply along branches for combined probabilities
Calculate the probability of a combined event using a sample space diagram and simplify the fraction
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw a tree diagram to map out all possible outcomes of a two-step probability situation — like flipping a coin and then rolling a die — and calculate the probability of any particular combination?

nodes.description: Construct and interpret Venn diagrams with two or three sets to organise and count outcomes; use systematic listing and the product rule for counting to enumerate all possible outcomes of combined events
evidence: Draw a two-circle Venn diagram to sort 30 students by whether they like football, like cricket, or like both
Shade the intersection A ∩ B and the union A ∪ B on a Venn diagram and explain what each region represents
Use a completed Venn diagram to calculate P(A), P(B), P(A ∩ B), and P(A ∪ B)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} surveys a class about which sports they play and draws a Venn diagram to show the results, can they use it to find out how many students play both sports — and calculate the probability of picking one of those students at random?

nodes.description: Represent ratio and proportion problems using bar models (rectangular strips divided into equal parts labelled with quantities) and tape diagrams (segmented strips showing part-to-part and part-to-whole relationships); use these visual models to set up and solve unequal sharing, scaling, and percentage problems — drawing the diagram first, then reading off the answer
evidence: Draw a bar model to represent a ratio problem — e.g. sharing £20 in the ratio 3:2 by drawing 5 equal blocks
Use a bar model to solve a proportion problem and explain each step
Compare bar models with other representations (tables, double number lines) and explain when each is most useful
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to share 30 stickers between two friends in a 2:3 ratio, can they draw a bar model — splitting a strip into 5 equal boxes — and use it to work out each share without just guessing?

nodes.displayName: 比、比例与百分数的语言
nodes.description: Know and use the vocabulary of ratio and proportion — ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, unequal, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole, and out of — and understand the difference between ratio (comparing parts to parts) and proportion (comparing a part to the whole)
evidence: Explain the difference between a 'ratio' and a 'proportion' using a concrete example like mixing paint
Use 'per cent' correctly and convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages in context
Define 'scale factor' and use it to describe how a shape has been enlarged or reduced
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is sharing something 3 ways and 2 ways, can they explain the difference between a ratio (like 3:2) and a proportion (like 3 out of 5) — showing they know what each word means?

nodes.description: Solve problems involving the calculation of percentages of amounts (e.g. 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison
evidence: Calculate 15% of 360 by finding 10% and 5% and combining
Compare two discounts given as percentages of different original prices
Explain a strategy for finding any percentage of an amount using known percentage facts
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a jumper originally costs £40 and is 15% off, can {{name}} work out how much the discount is and what the sale price would be?

nodes.description: Solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts
evidence: If the ratio of red to blue beads is 3:5 and there are 15 blue beads, find the number of red beads
Use multiplication facts to find the missing value: 'For every 2 apples there are 5 oranges; if there are 20 oranges, how many apples?'
Explain the multiplicative relationship between two quantities in a ratio context
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 3 eggs for every 200g of flour, can {{name}} work out how many eggs would be needed for 600g of flour?

nodes.description: Solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found
evidence: Find the missing side of a similar rectangle given a scale factor of 3
Determine the scale factor between two similar triangles from given side lengths
Use a scale factor to enlarge or reduce a shape and verify that all sides are in the same ratio
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a scale drawing where 1 cm represents 5 m, and a room measures 3.5 cm on the plan, can they work out the real length of the room?

nodes.displayName: 用分数与倍数解决不等分问题
nodes.description: Solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples
evidence: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5
Solve: 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam gets three times as many as Jo. If there are 30 altogether, how many does each get?'
Use fraction knowledge to explain why sharing in ratio 2:3 means one person gets 2/5 of the total
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If three friends share a bag of 24 sweets so that one person gets twice as many as each of the others, can {{name}} work out how many each person receives?

nodes.description: Use compound units such as speed (distance ÷ time), unit pricing (cost ÷ quantity), and density (mass ÷ volume); solve problems involving compound units
evidence: Calculate average speed given distance and time, converting between km/h and m/s if needed
Compare unit prices of two products sold in different quantities to find the better deal
Use the density formula to find mass, volume, or density given the other two values
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a car travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours, can {{name}} work out its average speed — and use the same idea to solve problems about price per kilogram or density of a material?

nodes.description: Divide a given quantity into two parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express the division as a fraction of the whole
evidence: Share £60 between two people in the ratio 2:3 by finding the value of one part
Express the result of sharing 24 sweets as 10 and 14 in ratio form as 5:7
Solve problems involving three-part ratios (e.g. divide 180 in the ratio 1:2:3)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If £60 is shared between two people in the ratio 2:3, can {{name}} work out how much each person gets?

nodes.sourceTitle: 一个量占另一个量的几分之几
nodes.displayName: 一个量占另一个量的几分之几
nodes.description: Express one quantity as a fraction of another where the result may be less than 1 or greater than 1, and interpret the meaning in context
evidence: Express 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours (= 3/8)
Express a larger quantity as a fraction of a smaller one and explain why the result exceeds 1
Simplify the resulting fraction and interpret its meaning in the original context
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If there are 15 boys and 20 girls in a class, can {{name}} express the number of boys as a fraction of the whole class and say whether that fraction is less than or greater than a half?

nodes.displayName: 百分数、分数与小数的关系及应用
nodes.description: Define percentage as 'number of parts per hundred'; interpret percentages and percentage changes as a fraction or a decimal; express one quantity as a percentage of another; compare quantities using percentages; work with percentages greater than 100%
evidence: Convert fluently between percentages, fractions, and decimals
Express one quantity as a percentage of another
Calculate percentage increases and decreases and interpret percentages greater than 100%
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a shop says a TV is 130% of its original price, does {{name}} understand what that means — and can they work out the new price from the original?

nodes.description: Know and use advanced vocabulary of multiplicative reasoning — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — accurately in problem-solving contexts
evidence: Distinguish between 'direct proportion' and 'inverse proportion' with real-world examples
Use 'rate', 'speed', and 'density' correctly and explain what units they are measured in
Calculate using compound measures — e.g. work out the speed of a car that travels 120 miles in 2 hours
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is solving a problem about speed or density, can they explain what 'compound unit' means and tell the difference between direct proportion (more of one means more of the other) and inverse proportion (more of one means less of the other)?

nodes.displayName: 比例表、双数轴与正比例图像
nodes.description: Represent proportional relationships using double number lines (two parallel number lines aligned at 0) and ratio tables; recognise that equivalent ratios generate straight lines through the origin when graphed
evidence: Plot pairs of proportional values on a coordinate grid and draw the straight line through the origin
Explain why a directly proportional relationship always passes through (0,0)
Read a proportion graph to find an unknown value — e.g. 'If 3 kg costs £6, how much does 5 kg cost?'
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is comparing the cost of buying different numbers of cinema tickets, can they sketch a proportion graph — a straight line through zero — and use it to read off the cost of any number of tickets without recalculating each time?

nodes.description: Use ratio notation to describe the relationship between two or more quantities, simplify ratios to their simplest form, and convert between ratio and fraction representations
evidence: Write a ratio from a word problem and simplify it (e.g. 12:8 = 3:2)
Convert a ratio to equivalent fractions of a whole (e.g. 3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5)
Simplify ratios involving decimals or fractions by finding a common multiplier
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a smoothie recipe uses orange juice and mango juice in the ratio 3:2, can {{name}} simplify that ratio, express it as a fraction, and work out how much of each is needed for a given total amount?

nodes.description: Use a scale, given as a ratio (e.g. 1:50), as a statement such as '1 cm represents 2 m', or as a scale factor, to work out actual lengths from a scale drawing or map and drawing lengths from actual lengths; reproduce a scale drawing at a different scale by finding each new drawing length, either through the actual length or from the ratio of the two scales; and solve map, room-plan and design problems with consistent units, converting between mm, cm, m and km before or after scaling. Areas from scale drawings and the area factor are developed in the follow-on topic Area from scale drawings
evidence: On a 1:50 room plan, find that a 9 cm wall is 450 cm = 4.5 m long, and that a 1.2 m doorway should be drawn 2.4 cm wide
Redraw a 1:50 plan at 1:100 by halving every drawing length (the 9 cm wall becomes 4.5 cm), and check one length by converting it back to the actual 4.5 m
Find the real distance between two towns 6.5 cm apart on a 1:25,000 map and give it in kilometres (162,500 cm = 1.625 km)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a house plan where 1 cm stands for 50 cm, could they work out how long a 9 cm wall really is — and redraw the plan half the size to fit a smaller sheet of paper?

nodes.description: Convert freely between related standard units of measurement (time, length, area, volume/capacity, mass) using decimal notation to up to three decimal places where appropriate
evidence: Convert between area units such as cm² and m² using the square of the linear scale factor
Perform multi-step conversions (e.g. convert 2.5 hours to seconds via minutes)
Convert volume units such as cm³ to litres and explain the relationship
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} convert between units confidently — for example, changing kilometres to metres, kilograms to grams, or hours and minutes to just minutes — including multi-step problems?

nodes.description: Find actual areas from a scale drawing or map, either by converting each drawing length to an actual length before multiplying or by using the area factor; explain why, when every length is multiplied by a scale factor k, areas are multiplied by k² (both dimensions are scaled), and avoid the mistake of applying the length factor to an area; convert between square units consistently (e.g. 1 m² = 10,000 cm²); and apply this to map, room-plan and design problems such as flooring, turf, paint or land area
evidence: Find the actual floor area of a room drawn 6 cm × 4 cm on a 1:50 plan by converting to 3 m × 2 m (6 m²), and check it with the area factor 50² = 2,500 (24 cm² × 2,500 = 60,000 cm² = 6 m²)
Show by drawing that enlarging a 2 cm × 1 cm rectangle by scale factor 3 gives a 6 cm × 3 cm rectangle containing 9 copies of the original, so the area factor is 3² = 9, not 3
Find the real area of a park shown as 8 cm² on a 1:10,000 map (8 × 10,000² cm² = 80,000 m²), giving the answer in square metres
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a room is drawn 6 cm by 4 cm on a plan where 1 cm stands for 50 cm, could {{name}} work out how much carpet the real room needs — and explain why a room twice as long and twice as wide would need four times as much carpet, not twice as much?

nodes.displayName: 百分数的应用 · 增减、原值与利息
nodes.description: Solve problems involving percentage increase, percentage decrease, finding the original value after a percentage change, and calculating simple interest
evidence: Calculate a 15% increase on £240 using a decimal multiplier (× 1.15)
Find the original price before a 20% discount resulted in a sale price of £64
Calculate simple interest on £500 at 3% per annum for 4 years
nodes.assessmentPrompt: If a bike originally costs £250 and its price goes up by 8%, can {{name}} work out the new price — and if a savings account earns 3% simple interest per year, how much interest would £500 earn in 4 years?

nodes.description: Recognise and solve problems involving direct proportion (as one quantity increases, the other increases at a constant rate) and inverse proportion (as one increases, the other decreases), including graphical and algebraic representations
evidence: Identify whether a real-world relationship is direct or inverse proportion and justify the choice
Set up and solve a direct-proportion equation (e.g. if 4 pens cost £6, find the cost of 10)
Sketch graphs showing direct proportion (straight line through origin) and inverse proportion (curve)
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand the difference between quantities that grow together at the same rate (direct proportion) and ones where one goes up as the other goes down — like more workers meaning fewer days to finish a job (inverse proportion)?

nodes.description: Understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio; use ratio notation; simplify ratios
evidence: Explain why 'for every 2 red beads there are 5 blue beads' can be written as 2:5 or as 2/5 of the blue count
Identify the multiplicative relationship in a table of values (e.g. y is always 3 times x)
Connect the ratio a:b to the fraction a/b and to the linear function y = (a/b)x
nodes.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why a ratio like 3:4 is really the same as the fraction ¾ — and show how that relationship connects to a straight-line graph through the origin?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Use mathematical words carefully when counting, comparing, and describing shapes and positions
evidence: Use 'more than', 'fewer than', and 'the same as' correctly when comparing groups
Name shapes correctly and describe their features using words like 'sides' and 'corners'
Use positional words (above, below, next to) precisely to describe where objects are
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} talks about maths — like comparing numbers or describing shapes — do they use the right words, like "larger than", "fewer", "beside", or "corner"?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Notice when a calculation or pattern repeats and use this to count more efficiently or predict results
evidence: Notice that skip counting by 2s follows a repeating odd/even pattern
Recognise that adding 1 to any number always gives the next counting number
Use a repeated pattern (e.g. +10 on a hundred chart always moves down one row) to predict answers
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is counting or doing repeated additions, have they started to notice the pattern — like "5, 10, 15, 20…" — and used it to predict the next number without counting one by one?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Select and use familiar tools (concrete objects, fingers, ten frames) to help solve a mathematical problem
evidence: Choose cubes, counters, or fingers to help solve an addition or subtraction problem
Use a ten frame to organise objects for counting or comparing
Explain why a particular tool (e.g. cubes rather than fingers) was chosen for a given problem
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is working out a maths problem, do they reach for helpful tools — like using their fingers, counters, or a number line — to support their thinking?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Make sense of a problem by identifying what is being asked, choosing concrete objects or pictures to represent the situation, and explaining a pathway to the solution
evidence: When given a word problem within 10, explain what the problem is asking before attempting to solve
Choose objects, fingers, or drawings to represent a problem situation
After finding an answer, check it makes sense (e.g. re-count objects to verify a total)
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} gets a maths problem they don't immediately know how to solve, do they stop and think about what the question is asking — maybe drawing a picture — before diving in?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Move between a real-world situation and a mathematical representation using concrete objects, drawings, diagrams, tables, number sentences, or bar models
evidence: Given a story about combining groups, represent it with counters or cubes and find the total
Given a set of objects, tell a simple addition or subtraction story to match
Connect a physical action (putting together, taking away) to the matching operation
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is working out a real-life maths problem — like sharing 8 sweets between 2 people — can they use objects or draw a picture to show what's happening before writing any numbers?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Show and tell how a mathematical answer was found using objects, drawings, and spoken words
evidence: Use objects or drawings to demonstrate how an addition or subtraction was solved
Respond to 'how do you know?' by pointing to objects or a drawing and describing what was done
Listen to a peer's explanation and say whether they agree or disagree
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: After {{name}} solves a maths problem, can they explain how they got their answer — using counters, a drawing, or words — rather than just writing down the final number?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Notice simple patterns and structures: spot that changing order doesn't change the total, and recognise how numbers relate to each other
evidence: Notice that 3 + 2 gives the same answer as 2 + 3 (early commutativity)
Recognise that teen numbers are 'ten and some more' (e.g. 14 is 10 and 4)
Spot a pattern in a sequence of objects or numbers and predict what comes next
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} noticed that adding numbers in a different order gives the same answer — like 3 + 5 and 5 + 3 both equal 8 — and can they explain why that makes sense?

separateMathThinkingNodes.sourceName: Using objects to model real problems
separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Use objects, drawings, or simple number sentences to represent a real-world situation (early mathematical modelling)
evidence: Draw a picture or use objects to represent a simple real-world situation involving counting or comparing
Write or dictate a number sentence to describe a real-world situation (e.g. 'I had 5 apples and ate 2')
Use the model to answer a question about the situation
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: If you describe a simple real-life situation to {{name}} — like "there are 3 birds on a fence and 2 more land" — can they write a number sentence like 3 + 2 = 5 to represent it?

separateMathThinkingNodes.sourceTitle: 把数学与生活联系起来
separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Represent real-world problems with number sentences, bar models, or diagrams, and interpret the mathematical result back in context
evidence: Choose and write an appropriate number sentence for a measurement or money word problem
Draw a bar model or diagram to represent a two-step or comparison problem
Interpret the numerical answer in context (e.g. '15 cm means the ribbon is 15 centimetres long')
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} solves a word problem by drawing a bar model or writing an equation, can they also explain what their answer means in the real-world context — like "that means each child gets 4 sweets"?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Move between real-world situations, drawings, and number sentences, explaining how each representation connects to the others (quantitative reasoning)
evidence: Write a number sentence (e.g. 14 + 5 = 19) to match a word problem and explain the connection
Draw a bar model or part-whole diagram to represent a problem, then solve using the diagram
Translate between a concrete model and a symbolic equation, describing what each number represents
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} solves a word problem, can they draw a diagram or write a number sentence to show their thinking — and then explain how the picture and the numbers match the real situation?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: With teacher prompting, explain and justify mathematical reasoning using drawings, number sentences, or words
evidence: Explain a solution strategy using a drawing or number sentence (e.g. 'I made ten first, then added the rest')
Justify why an answer is correct by showing an alternative method that gives the same result
Identify and explain an error in a worked example or a peer's solution
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} "how did you work that out?", can they show you with a drawing or explain their steps in simple words?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: spot calculation patterns, describe rules for sequences, and predict results using known mathematical facts
evidence: Use a known doubles fact to derive a near-doubles answer (e.g. 6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1 = 13)
Notice that subtracting 10 from any two-digit number always reduces the tens digit by 1
Describe a rule for a pattern and use it to extend or predict (e.g. 'each time we add 5, the ones digit alternates between 0 and 5')
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is practising times tables or number patterns, do they spot a shortcut — like "if 6 × 7 = 42, then 6 × 8 must be 48" — and use known facts to work out ones they haven't memorised yet?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: With teacher guidance, make sense of multi-step and more complex problems by planning a pathway to the solution, identifying relevant information, and choosing appropriate operations
evidence: When given a word problem within 20 or 100, identify the known information and what needs to be found
Try a strategy (drawing, number line, known fact) and switch approach if the first attempt stalls
Check the reasonableness of an answer using estimation or a different method
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out that 3 children each get 12 sweets and ends up with 5, does {{name}} pause and say "that doesn't seem right" rather than just writing it down?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Select and use appropriate tools and representations (number lines, hundred squares, rulers, part-whole models) to support problem-solving
evidence: Choose a number line or hundred square to support adding or subtracting two-digit numbers
Select a ruler when a problem requires measuring length
Explain why one representation (e.g. a number line vs cubes) is more helpful for a particular problem
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is tackling a maths problem, do they choose a useful tool — like a number line for addition or a hundred square to count on — rather than always working in their head?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct vocabulary, specify units, and use symbols accurately
evidence: Use the = sign correctly to mean 'is the same as' rather than 'the answer is'
Include units when giving a measurement answer (e.g. '12 cm' not just '12')
Use precise terms such as 'edge', 'vertex', 'face' when describing 3-D shapes, and 'greater than', 'less than' when comparing numbers
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes or talks about a maths answer, do they include the units — like "5 centimetres" rather than just "5" — and use the right symbols like = or <?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Look for and use mathematical structure: apply properties of operations, place-value patterns, and relationships between shapes to solve problems efficiently
evidence: Use the commutative property deliberately (e.g. reorder 3 + 9 as 9 + 3 to count on from the larger number)
Use place-value structure to add or subtract tens (e.g. 47 + 10 = 57 because only the tens digit changes)
Recognise structural similarities between shapes (e.g. rectangles and squares both have 4 sides and 4 right angles)
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} notices a pattern in their maths work — like how multiplying by 10 always adds a zero — do they use that pattern to solve similar problems more quickly?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Select and use appropriate tools and representations strategically, including choosing between mental methods, jottings, formal algorithms, and calculators for arithmetic with multi-digit numbers, decimals, and fractions
evidence: Choose a mental method for 345 + 200 but a written method for 345 + 278
Select a ruler vs a metre stick based on the object being measured
Decide when a number line is more useful than base-ten blocks for a given problem
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} faces a maths problem, do they think about which method suits it best — like doing easy ones in their head, using a written method for bigger calculations, or sketching a diagram for geometry?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: extend multiplication table patterns, derive unknown facts from known ones, and describe rules for sequences
evidence: Notice that all multiples of 4 are even and use this to check answers
Derive 8 × 7 from 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 by spotting the pattern
Describe a rule for a growing pattern (e.g. 'add 50 each time') and use it to predict the next terms
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is learning their times tables, do they use known facts to figure out ones they're not sure of — for example, using 5 × 6 = 30 to work out that 6 × 6 = 36?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Construct and follow multi-step mathematical arguments; identify errors in reasoning and explain why a method works or does not work
evidence: Explain step by step why a columnar addition method gives the correct answer
Find and explain an error in a worked example (e.g. incorrect regrouping)
Construct a simple argument for why a general statement is true (e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number')
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears another child's explanation for how they solved a maths problem, can {{name}} say whether the reasoning makes sense — and if not, point out exactly where the logic goes wrong?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: With teacher support, make sense of multi-step problems involving larger numbers or mixed operations by breaking them into parts, choosing strategies, and checking answers for reasonableness — children at this stage are developing the habit with guidance; independent strategy evaluation comes later
evidence: Break a two-step word problem within 1000 into sub-problems and solve each part
Estimate an answer before calculating to set a reasonableness benchmark
Check an answer using a different method or inverse operation and revise if needed
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets an answer that seems way too big or too small for a maths problem, do they notice and go back to check, even without you pointing it out?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Look for and use mathematical structure: apply place-value patterns to three-digit operations, use multiplication/division relationships, and exploit shape properties to classify
evidence: Use the structure of place value to explain why adding hundreds only changes the hundreds digit
Use commutativity and the relationship between multiplication and division to derive unknown facts
Classify shapes by their structural properties (number of sides, right angles, parallel lines)
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is multiplying or working with larger numbers, do they use what they know about place value or number relationships to simplify the calculation — like breaking 24 × 3 into 20 × 3 + 4 × 3?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, and symbolic equations involving three-digit numbers and fractions, explaining what each part represents
evidence: Write an equation with three-digit numbers to match a measurement or money word problem
Draw a bar model to represent a fraction problem and use it to solve
Explain how a number line diagram relates to the quantities in a word problem
separateMathThinkingNodes.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} works through a maths problem involving fractions or three-digit numbers, can they switch between drawing a diagram, using a number line, and writing an equation — and explain what each one shows?

separateMathThinkingNodes.description: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct place-value and fraction vocabulary, specify units in measurement answers, and use notation accurately
